Together they show even the friendliest post worked into the same tight system as London and Paris. Even friendly posts were kept to the same tight system of orders and reports. A tight system, fairly run, asked no post to bear the war alone.
frus-1861-d300:
Guidance for Mr. Dickinson left Washington on 5 June 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 300 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d100:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 12 July 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 100 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d200:
A second Seward note to Lord Lyons dated 7 January 1862 appears as Document 200 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Sending two notes in a day was routine when separate matters each needed their own paper.

With the Trent crisis ending, the two men faced a pile of lesser frictions left by a year of war. Stopped ships, detained men, and hard words in the press. Notes like these handled that residue one case at a time. They show diplomacy returning to its ordinary pace after a brush with war. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d300:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed William L. Dayton in Paris on 4 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 300 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The date also carries two Dayton reports, so the mails crossed.

Crossing traffic was heavy that summer because events outran the steamers: Bull Run was three weeks away, and Antietam six. Seward wrote to Paris in the dark about the fall campaign, as Dayton wrote to him. The same-date papers in the file show two governments reasoning from different facts toward the same questions. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d400:
An instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Horace J. Perry in Madrid under the date 22 February 1862. It stands as Document 400 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, which accompanied the President's annual message to Congress.

By February 1862 Union armies were winning in the West, and Seward wanted foreign courts to hear of it from his own men first. Spain, holding Cuba just off the Confederate coast, could help or harm the Union cause. Orders of this kind told the Madrid legation what facts to stress and what claims to answer. They did so week by week, as the war's news reached Europe.
frus-1862-d500:
On 10 May 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The note is Document 500 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

A next-day follow-up usually carried a correction, an enclosure, or a point that could not wait for the weekly pouch. In May 1862 the points that could not wait often concerned ships. They might be a raider fitting out, or a blockade runner in a Dutch colonial port. They might be a ruling to be sought. Seward's habit of writing twice in two days to a minor post shows how seriously the Department took the maritime war. The note is small; the system it reveals is not.
frus-1862-d600:
On 25 December 1861 Spain's minister of state wrote again to the Spanish representatives in Paris and London. The letter is Document 600 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in the Spanish appendix on Mexico.

A second circular within five days suggests fast-moving allied business that Christmas week, as the expedition's landings in Mexico began. Madrid's envoys in Paris and London were its channels to the two senior partners in the venture, and they had to speak with one voice. For the modern reader, these internal Spanish papers are the volume's most unusual feature. They are the other side's orders. The State Department printed them so Congress could judge the Mexican affair from the actors' own instructions.
frus-1862-d700: Dated 29 July 1862, this paper came from the Secretaryship of Foreign Relations of Salvador, tied in its title with Nicaragua. It is document 700 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, among the Central America papers. The record names the sending office and the date, but no signer and no subject, so it is described at that level only.
frus-1863p1-d100:
This letter of 2 March 1863, from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, carries the round number 100 in the volume's count. It is the fourth of twelve Seward letters to Adams dated that day. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is in part one of the 1863 volume.

Milestone numbers mean little, but the batch behind this one means much. On a single day Seward laid out the London brief head by head, in a dozen short sheets. Adams could then take each point to the British in its turn. This letter is a mid-batch piece, valued as part of the most packed day in the whole printed exchange.
frus-1863p1-d200:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 18 May 1863. The letter is document 200 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d300:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 28 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 300 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d400:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 23 February 1863. The note is document 400 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d500:
The letter printed as document 500 was written on 8 May 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d600:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington received a letter dated 3 August 1863 from Secretary William H. Seward. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late summer of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pone-0000100:
Justin A. Harris, Ehsan Arabzadeh, Adrienne L. Fairhall, and their team studied the sense of touch in PLOS ONE in 2006. People can tell apart vibrations of different frequencies through the skin of the fingers. The team tested what limits that skill, such as how strong the vibration feels versus how often it repeats.

Their results bear on how the cortex codes touch: whether by the rate of firing, its timing, or both. That code is what a prosthetic hand would need to speak to feel natural. Careful measures of what people can and cannot tell apart set the spec for such devices. The paper links a lab measure of perception to real neural code questions.
plos-pone-0000200:
Milena Raffi and Ralph M. Siegel published this vision neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Optic flow is the streaming pattern of light across the eyes when we move through the world. The authors map how the inferior parietal lobule of a behaving monkey's brain organizes responses to that flow.

Optic flow tells an animal its heading, speed, and the layout around it. A functional architecture for flow in this brain region shows how the cortex divides that job. The work helps explain how primates, including humans, steer through space using vision alone.
plos-pone-0000300:
Xiao Xiao Jenny Gu, Feng Yun Yue, Colin M. Kovacs, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many cytokines, immune signal proteins, share one receptor part, the common gamma chain. The authors study the role of those cytokines in reversing T cell anergy. Anergy is the switched-off state of HIV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells in infected patients.

Anergic T cells are present but useless against the virus. If cytokine signals can wake them, that is a therapeutic opening. The paper tests which signals do the waking, informing immune-based strategies meant to restore the body's own control of HIV.
plos-pone-0000400:
Roser Pinyol and colleagues described a control circuit for nerve cell shape in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circuit involves N-WASP and the Arp2/3 complex, proteins that build branching scaffolds of actin, the cell's structural fiber. A third protein, Abp1, helps regulate them, and the team placed it in the pathway that shapes neurons.

A neuron's shape, its trunk of dendrites and its long axon, decides what it can connect to. Actin scaffolds push the membrane into those forms. Showing that Abp1 helps control the N-WASP and Arp2/3 machinery adds a link to the chain of command. That chain sculpts nerve cells as the brain wires itself.
plos-pone-0000500:
Dana Sumilo and colleagues challenged a popular explanation for a disease surge in the Baltic states, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Tick-borne encephalitis, a viral brain infection spread by ticks, rose sharply in the Baltics in the 1990s. Climate change was often blamed, since warmer weather favors ticks. The team's title states their finding: climate change cannot explain the upsurge.

Ruling out the easy explanation redirects attention to social and land-use changes after the Soviet era, which altered farming, forests, and human contact with ticks. The paper is a caution against attributing every disease shift to climate without checking the numbers, and it models how to test such claims.
plos-pone-0000600:
Cristina A. Faria and colleagues found a weakness in a flagship farm technology, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bt maize is engineered to poison caterpillar pests. The team found a chain of effects. Bt maize is highly open to aphid attack, so aphids thrive on it. The wasps that attack caterpillar pests feed on the aphids' honeydew. With more food, the wasps perform better against the pests.

The chain is indirect: a pest the plant cannot stop ends up feeding the allies that kill the pests it can. Such side effects decide whether engineered crops help or hinder biological control in real fields. The study is a reminder that fields are food webs, not single-trait demonstrations.
plos-pone-0000700:
Julio Echegoyen, Axel Neu, Kevin D. Graber and colleagues studied how brain circuits steady their state after activity is blocked. Their 2007 PLOS ONE work concerns homeostatic plasticity, the adjustments that keep circuits from becoming hyperactive or falling silent. Little was known about this process after activity changes in vivo, inside a living animal.

Blocking activity in the hippocampus, they studied synaptic scaling, where synapses strengthen or weaken all at once, and intrinsic plasticity of the neurons. Age-dependence was part of the question too. Brains that cannot regain balance in activity are prone to disorders like epilepsy. Knowing how the balance is restored, and how it changes with age, guides that research.
plos-pone-0000800:
Stephen B. Beres and James M. Musser catalogued the borrowed genes in the group A Streptococcus metagenome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Strains of one bacterial species differ in gene content, and those differences drive medically relevant traits such as virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Group A Streptococcus causes a diverse array of human infections and after-effects, and shows complex population structure.

Exogenous genetic elements, DNA arrived from outside, are their focus: genes picked up from viruses and other bacteria. Such imports can turn a mild strain dangerous in one step. Tallying their contribution to the species' total gene pool explains how one species produces so many disease patterns.
plos-pone-0000900:
Gang Li, Jinhong Wang, Stephen Rossiter and colleagues found fast change in the FoxP2 gene in echolocating bats, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. FoxP2 helps control the face and mouth movements behind speech and calls. Across backboned animals it barely changes, yet humans and chimps differ at two building blocks.

Bats that hunt by sound place huge demands on mouth and voice control. The team compared FoxP2 across bat species and report sped up evolution in the echolocating lines. The result links a speech related gene to another group that lives by precise vocal skill. It widens the story of how vocal control evolves.
plos-pone-0001000:
Logan Walsh, Deanna Carere, Colin Cooper and colleagues tracked two tissue remodeling partners through frog metamorphosis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Matrix metalloproteinases cut up the material around cells, and their inhibitors, TIMPs, keep them in check. Together they rebuild tissue, and TIMPs also help switch some enzymes on.

In the frog Xenopus laevis, metamorphosis rebuilds nearly everything, from tail to gut. The team found RNA levels of one enzyme, MT1-MMP, and its inhibitor TIMP-2 mimic each other across that change. Matched timing suggests the pair are managed as a unit. The frog gives a whole body view of remodeling that cell cultures cannot.
plos-pone-0001100:
Ruvandhi Nathavitharana, Jorge Coronel and David Moore tested sunlight for making TB culture waste safe, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disposing of TB culture material is a real problem in poor settings. Cultures multiply the infectious load of patient samples greatly before they are thrown away.

Solar cookers had already shown they can kill conventional bacteria. The team examine solar disinfection of MODS mycobacterial cultures, a low cost TB culture method. Sunlight is the one resource many poor clinics have in surplus. If a solar cooker can sterilize culture waste, a safety step that rich labs automate becomes possible where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0001200:
In a complex system, it is often unclear which parts to adjust to improve performance. Di Wu, Elizabeth Townsley, and Alan Tartakoff present a selection strategy for that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their test bed is the cell, where the components that most affect a trait are rarely obvious.

The authors describe covert genetic selections to optimize phenotypes, ways of letting a population of cells reveal which molecular targets matter most. The method identifies and prioritizes targets rather than testing guesses one by one. The same logic, they note, applies to other high-complexity systems, from institutions to economies.
plos-pone-0001300:
Interleukin-24, also known as mda-7, is a signaling protein said to kill tumor cells while sparing normal ones. Stephanie Kreis and colleagues tested a lab-made version against melanoma cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. IL-24 belongs to the IL-10 family of cytokines and is produced by certain immune cells.

The authors report that recombinant interleukin-24 lacks apoptosis-inducing traits in melanoma cells. A result like this matters: it tests a hopeful claim in the cancer literature and warns against building therapy plans on it without care. Their study used the purified protein itself, rather than gene delivery.
plos-pone-0001400:
Bernard Couvreur and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on tick proteins that blunt the host defense. Ticks feed on blood for a long time, so they must calm host blood clotting, swelling, and immune attack. They do so with a suite of spit proteins from large gene families. The team studied one family that blocks a key defense arm.

The authors describe how members of this family vary and how each one acts. Small shifts in form lead to shifts in target and strength. The work maps a key tool ticks use to stay attached and feed. It may also point to new ways to foil ticks and the ills they spread.
plos-pone-0001500:
Emily Manderson, Mohan Malleshaiah, and Stephen Michnick published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a yeast gene of unknown job. More than a thousand yeast genes still lack a clear role, despite vast data on gene use and protein links. The team built a screen that merges gene tests with protein link data. They used it to probe one such gene.

Their screen ties the gene, called Elm1, to shutting off a yeast growth factor. A new job for an old gene shows the screen works. The same tack can be run on the rest of the unknown list. That promises a faster close to the yeast gene map.
plos-pone-0001600:
Asako Shindo, Takamasa Yamamoto, and Naoto Ueno wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell polarity in frog embryos. Polarity, the built in top and bottom of a cell, shapes how embryos form. In frog gastrulation, gut layer cells line up and slide past each other. That slide stretches the embryo from head to tail. The team tracked how polarity is set in step across the sheet.

Their work maps the cues that align cells as the sheet moves. A shared alignment is what lets the whole tissue stretch in one course. Faults here cause grave birth defects. The frog model gives a clear view of a step all backboned embryos share.
plos-pone-0001700:
Denise M. Wolf, Lisa Fontaine-Bodin, Ilka Bischofs, and their co-authors measured memory in a bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Memory is usually credited to higher organisms. But many bacterial control networks show complex dynamics and multi-stable behavior. Those traits are linked to memory in other systems, and bacteria plainly respond to their own past states.

The team quantified history-dependent behavior: how a cell's response to a signal depends on what it met before. The full text gives the experiments, the time scales of the effect, and the model they built. A measured bacterial memory gives a concrete system for studying how single cells store information about their past. It also has uses in engineering microbes that remember exposures.
plos-pone-0001800:
Alfonso J. C. Soler Bistué, Daniel Birshan, Andrew P. Tomaras, and their co-authors sequenced a resistance plasmid in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The spread of antimicrobial resistance genes is an important public health and biodefense threat. Plasmids, small DNA circles that jump between bacteria, drive the rapid acquisition of resistance by pathogens.

The paper gives the nucleotide sequence of pMET1, a multiresistance plasmid from Klebsiella pneumoniae. It also gives its similarity to pCRY, a plasmid of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, and to integrative conjugative elements. The full text gives the gene map and the shared segments. Shared parts across plasmids of very different pathogens show how resistance genes travel.
plos-pone-0001900:
John Lin and co-authors tested hunger-boosting drugs in monkeys in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The drugs switch on TrkB, a cell receptor tied to body weight. When this path fails, people and mice eat too much and gain great weight. When drugs in mice switch it on, food intake and weight drop.

The team gave TrkB-switching drugs through the body, not the brain, to non-human primates. As the title states, appetite rose and the animals gained weight, the reverse of the mouse results. That clash across species is a warning for drug work: a path that trims weight in mice may not do the same in primates.
plos-pone-0002000:
Anavaj Sakuntabhai and co-authors hunted host genes that shape malaria in Senegal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Attacks of falciparum malaria range from mild to deadly, even in the same region. Good evidence says genes of the person, not just the parasite, drive part of that range.

Most gene hunts had used a case and control design, which has limits. The team instead mapped traits tied to malaria to spots in the genome in Senegalese families, and tested how strongly each trait is inherited. Family maps of this kind can find protective genes that case studies miss.
plos-pone-0002100:
Judith Legrand and co-authors modeled tuberculosis control in crowded prisons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. TB in prisons is a major health problem in countries with high or middling rates, such as Brazil. For operational reasons, control strategies in prisons cannot be compared through population-based intervention studies, since prisons cannot be run as trial sites at will.

A mathematical model is proposed to compare strategies instead, in highly endemic, overcrowded prisons. Models can weigh screening, isolation, and treatment options before scarce funds are spent. Prison TB spills into the wider public, so gains inside walls count outside them too.
plos-pone-0002200:
Jason Bourke and co-authors built a 3D model of a dingo skull to test bite physics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jaw models predict that bite force depends on how wide the jaw opens and on which tooth does the biting. Few studies had checked those predictions in a real mammal, and none had weighed the role of gape angle.

The team used a finite element approach, which breaks the skull into many small pieces in a computer. They computed bite force and skull stress across gapes and tooth positions. Their results test long-used jaw models against hard numbers from an iconic Australian predator.
plos-pone-0002300:
Darren Soanes, Intikhab Alam, Mike Cornell, and co-authors compared the genomes of fungi and their kin across many species, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fungi and oomycetes cause many of the most serious diseases of plants, from potato blight to tree diebacks. A shared genomic pattern might explain what makes them good pathogens.

The team analyzed genome sequences from thirty-six species, including seven plant pathogenic ones. They looked for gene families that had expanded in the pathogenic lines. Expanded families are candidate tool kits for infecting plants, and each one offers targets for crop protection that go beyond spraying single chemicals.
plos-pone-0002400:
Holt and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alison R. Holt, Zoe G. Davies, Claire Tyler, and others. Its subject is meta-Analysis of the Effects of Predation on Animal Prey Abundance: Evidence from UK Vertebrates. Controlling vertebrate predators is one of the most widespread forms of wildlife management and it continues to cause conflict between stakeholders worldwide.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002500:
Led by Haslam, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Niall J. Haslam, Nava E. Whiteford, Gerald Weber, and others. Its subject is optimal Probe Length Varies for Targets with High Sequence Variation. The title goes on to note implications for Probe Library Design for Resequencing Highly Variable Genes. Sequencing by hybridisation is an effective method for obtaining large amounts of DNA sequence information at low cost.

The efficiency of SBH depends on the design of the probe library to provide the maximum information for minimum cost. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002600:
Research by Wei and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yan Wei, Mei-Hua Qu, Xing-Sheng Wang, and others. Its subject is binding to the Minor Groove of the Double-Strand, Tau Protein Prevents DNA from Damage by Peroxidation. Tau, an important microtubule linked protein, has been found to bind to DNA.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002700:
Work by David Caramelli and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a 28,000 years old Cro-Magnon mtDNA sequence differs from all potentially contaminating modern sequences. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David Caramelli, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. DNA sequences from ancient speciments may in fact result from undetected contamination of the ancient specimens by modern DNA. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002800:
Research from Shinobu Ueda and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers establishment of rat embryonic stem cells and making of chimera rats. The catalog record names Shinobu Ueda first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The rat is a reference animal model for physiological studies and for the analysis of multigenic human diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, neurological disorders. The authors add a further point. The rats have long been used in extensive chemical carcinogenesis studies. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002900:
Philip Monahan, Kevin de Souza and William Idsardi used brain imaging in 2008 to time how listeners restore a missing pitch. When the lowest tone of a complex sound is absent, hearers still sense it. When the brain rebuilds that missing fundamental was still unclear.

Their MEG recordings, which track fast magnetic signals from the brain, placed the recovery in auditory cortex within 100 milliseconds of the sound. That is a tight time bound from the study itself. Hearing scientists get a clearer timeline for one of the basic tricks that lets us judge pitch and voice.
plos-pone-0003000:
Etienne Morel, Stéphane Fouquet, Carine Strup-Perrot and co-authors studied the cellular prion protein in epithelial cells in 2008. The normal prion protein, PrPc, is found throughout the body, yet its everyday function was still debated. Most work had focused on the nervous system, leaving epithelia poorly investigated.

The team had earlier found PrPc targeted to cell-cell junctions in polarized epithelial cells. Their PLOS ONE study reports it is involved in epithelial cell proliferation and in placing junction proteins. That widens the prion protein's normal job beyond the brain, a useful baseline for disease work.
plos-pone-0003100:
Ildefonso De La Fuente, Luis Martínez, Alberto Pérez-Samartín and co-authors argued in 2008 that cell metabolism self-organizes globally. For many years enzymes were assumed to work either alone or in small catalytic groups. Studies using metabolic network models were helping to reveal the functional complexity of enzyme dynamics.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors present evidence for global self-organization of the cellular metabolic structure. That view treats metabolism as one coordinated system, not a bag of separate pathways. It changes how models of cell chemistry should be built and tested. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003200:
Paola Ferrante, Claudia Catalanotti, Giulia Bonente and colleagues build a regulated gene switch for an alga in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a model system for algal and cell biology and is used for biotechnology, such as molecular farming and biological hydrogen production. Its metal-responsive CYC6 promoter is repressed by copper and induced by nickel ions.

The team present an optimized, chemically regulated gene expression system for Chlamydomonas. Readers get a tighter on-off tool for a workhorse alga. Reliable switches matter when engineered algae must make a product only at the right stage of growth.
plos-pone-0003300:
Marilis Rodriguez and co-authors study a malaria parasite surface protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. To invade a red blood cell, Plasmodium falciparum must use many contacts between its own proteins and receptors on the cell. Finding those receptors is a major task in learning how invasion works, since each contact is a chance to block it.

The team describe PfRH5, a new member of a binding protein family, show it binds the red cell, and hunt for its receptor. Readers meet a parasite protein at the heart of cell entry. Entry proteins are top vaccine targets for blood-stage malaria.
plos-pone-0007400: Energy development in the American West spreads roads, wells, and pipelines across wildlife habitat. The researchers mapped where oil and gas drilling could go in the Intermountain West and estimated what it would cost native species. By connecting development potential directly to biodiversity impacts, the study gives land managers a way to weigh energy gains against harm to the region's animals.
plos-pone-0007500: Mice missing a stretch of chromosome covering two cystatin genes offered a window into blood formation. This study measured blood stem-cell activity and cystatin gene output in these mice. Cystatins block protein-chewing enzymes, so the results connect a family of enzyme inhibitors to how blood cells are made.
plos-pone-0007600: How does the brain's hearing center encode where a sound comes from? This study used magnetoencephalography to watch the human auditory cortex respond to sounds from different directions. The results favor a population rate code — the location read out from the combined firing of many neurons rather than a map of dedicated spots.
plos-pone-0007700: Furin is a molecular scissors that activates proteins involved in cancer and infection — making it a prized drug target. This study designed a new peptide inhibitor with an unusual enediyne structure that blocks furin from processing growth factors. The novel chemistry offers a fresh template for anti-cancer and antiviral drugs.
plos-pone-0007800: Chikungunya's joint pain can linger for months, eroding quality of life. This retrospective cohort study compared survivors with unexposed people and quantified the lasting burden. The numbers make the case that the virus's aftermath deserves medical attention long after the fever fades.
plos-pone-0007900: Inherited dementia got a mouse stand-in. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Giliberto's team built knock-in mice carrying FDD mutations. The BRI2 gene faults trigger brain decline. The mouse stand-in was characterized. The model feeds dementia research.
plos-pone-0008000: Migrating shorebirds refuel in farm fields. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by McCarty and colleagues watched buff-breasted sandpipers during migratory stopovers in agricultural fields. Modern farming reshapes the landscapes birds depend on. Understanding how the birds use crop fields is the first step to judging whether agriculture helps or harms their epic journeys.
plos-pone-0008100: Type 2 diabetes disrupts entire regulatory networks, not just single genes. This study used expression-based network biology to find the key pathways altered in diabetes and its complications. The network view points to master regulators worth targeting.
plos-pone-0008200: A devastating quake's toll on newborns was tallied. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Tan's team measured how the Wenchuan earthquake affected birth outcomes. Disasters strike pregnancies through stress, injury, and wrecked care. The birth records captured the quake's shadow on the next generation. The toll underscores why disaster plans must shield expectant mothers.
plos-pone-0008300: Some women never get urinary infections despite carrying bacteria. This study linked genetic variants in innate immune genes to asymptomatic bacteriuria. The DNA differences explain why the same bacteria cause disease in some and peace in others.
plos-pone-0008400: A fertility brake got a human ID. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Ubuka's team found the human versions of a gonadotropin-blocking hormone. Quail had revealed the original. The human IDs were mapped. The find feeds reproductive medicine.
